final_proof:
Let g = φ⁻¹ : A₂ → A₁. Since φ is bijective, its inverse g is also bijective: the identities g ∘ φ = id_A₁ and φ ∘ g = id_A₂ show that φ is the inverse of g. It remains to prove that g is a complete lattice homomorphism.

For i ∈ {1,2} and X ⊆ Aᵢ, write ⋁ᵢX and ⋀ᵢX for the supremum and infimum of X in Lᵢ, respectively. These exist for every X, including X = ∅, because the lattices are complete. Since φ is a complete lattice homomorphism, for every T ⊆ A₁,

φ(⋁₁T) = ⋁₂φ[T]  and  φ(⋀₁T) = ⋀₂φ[T],

where φ[T] = {φ(t) : t ∈ T}.

Now let S ⊆ A₂ be arbitrary and set T = g[S] = {g(s) : s ∈ S} ⊆ A₁. The inverse identities imply φ[T] = S: indeed, φ(g(s)) = s for every s ∈ S, and every member of φ[T] has this form. Hence preservation of arbitrary suprema by φ gives

φ(⋁₁g[S]) = φ(⋁₁T) = ⋁₂φ[T] = ⋁₂S.

Applying g to both sides and using g ∘ φ = id_A₁, we obtain

g(⋁₂S) = ⋁₁g[S].

Similarly, preservation of arbitrary infima by φ gives

φ(⋀₁g[S]) = ⋀₂φ[g[S]] = ⋀₂S,

and applying g yields

g(⋀₂S) = ⋀₁g[S].

Because S was arbitrary, these identities also cover the empty subset (and therefore preservation of top and bottom). Thus g = φ⁻¹ preserves all suprema and all infima, so it is a complete lattice homomorphism. Together with its bijectivity, this proves that φ⁻¹ : L₂ → L₁ is a bijective complete lattice homomorphism.
